Maladaptive Strategies.value: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred

Being reminded of the event by others

Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
I feel like an object, not like a person

vignette:
Anjali presents as a poised and articulate 24-year-old urban planner, but her composure is a carefully constructed façade. For years, she has navigated the world as if walking on a tripwire, a tension that dates back to a childhood spent in her aunt’s care. She struggles to deliberately recall the specifics of that time; when she tries, the narrative fragments, leaving her with a sense of hazy confusion. Yet, the emotional truth of it ambushes her without warning. Sometimes, standing on a crowded subway car, a wave of pure, disembodied rage will wash over her, hot and suffocating, with no accompanying image to explain its origin. It’s the same feeling that surfaces when she allows herself to think about how her aunt was never held accountable, a burning conviction that what happened was deeply unfair and the world simply looked away.

The abuse was quiet and methodical. She remembers being told to lie perfectly still on her bed for what her aunt called “inspections.” Under the cold light of the bedside lamp, she was scrutinized, her body treated less like a child’s and more like an object to be assessed for flaws. The memory of that clinical, detached gaze is what makes her job so difficult now. During community board presentations, standing at the podium with dozens of pairs of eyes on her, the feeling returns with paralyzing intensity. She is no longer Anjali, the professional explaining zoning variances; she is a thing being seen, evaluated, and found wanting. Her thoughts scatter, the carefully prepared notes on the lectern blurring into meaningless shapes, and she has to fight a rising tide of nausea that threatens to choke her. That feeling—the queasy, stomach-turning dread—is a faithful echo of the sickness she felt as a child, waiting for her aunt’s bedroom door to open.

Over the years, Anjali has developed a set of rigid, unspoken rules to manage this internal state of high alert. Her world has shrunk to a few select locations where she feels a semblance of safety: her small apartment, a specific corner booth at a local café, and her cubicle at work, provided no one stands behind her. Any sudden movement from a colleague in her peripheral vision—an arm raised too quickly, a chair pushed back abruptly—sends a jolt of alarm through her, and she has to clench her fists under her desk to keep from flinching. This avoidance extends to conversations with her own family. Her mother, perhaps sensing the unresolved pain, will sometimes try to bring up Anjali’s childhood, prefacing it with a hesitant, “I was thinking about when you lived with your aunt...” The moment the words are out, Anjali feels a wall of ice go up inside her. She will abruptly change the subject, feign a sudden headache, or simply end the phone call. It is an automatic, non-negotiable defense; she cannot bear to hear the story of her own life told back to her. To avoid conflict, which she equates with danger, she has become relentlessly agreeable. At work, she goes along with whatever her team leader suggests, even when she knows a project is headed in the wrong direction. It feels safer to be compliant, to make herself small and unthreatening. But each time she swallows her own opinion, a voice inside her whispers that this is proof of what she has long suspected: she is a weak person, incapable of standing up for herself.

She finds herself frequently lost in daydreams of another life, a parallel existence where she grew up differently. In these fantasies, she is confident, outspoken, and unafraid to take up space. The contrast between this imagined self and her reality is a source of profound sadness. She is single, having found the vulnerability of dating unbearable. The idea of being truly seen by a partner is terrifying. This sense of being an object rather than a person has calcified over time, a core belief that shapes her every interaction. The final impetus for seeking therapy was a routine notice from her doctor’s office about an overdue physical exam. The thought of lying on an examination table, subjected to a medical procedure under the bright, impersonal lights, was intolerable. It represented a complete loss of control, a horrifying reenactment of her past. Anjali came to her first session hoping, more than anything, to find a way to feel solid in her own skin, to believe she was a person who mattered and not just an object to be observed.
